Situation1: They set aside part of their routine to light a lamp and offer prayers at their home altar.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story:
Every morning, I rise before dawn, the scent of sandalwood and the soft glow of the lamp guiding me through my prayers at the home altar. As a Hindu, these rituals are not just tradition—they are my anchor, a way to honor my ancestors and seek clarity for the day ahead. But lately, my role as an advocate has begun to weigh heavily on me. I spend my days collecting stories of injustice, listening to people who have been wronged by the very systems meant to protect them. My evenings are filled with heated discussions, drafting petitions, and challenging officials who seem unmoved by suffering.

Today, a crucial meeting with community leaders is scheduled at the same time as my evening puja. My family expects me to uphold our rituals, to be present and reverent. My clients and colleagues expect me to be relentless, to show up and fight for change. As the clock ticks closer to both commitments, I feel the tension tightening in my chest. I stand at the threshold, torn between the quiet sanctity of my altar and the urgent call for justice echoing from the meeting hall, uncertain which path to take.
